body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… As we head into the United Nations’ 31st annual flagship climate conference (COP31), to be held next week in Antalya, Türkiye, greenwashing presents a large and growing problem in the private sector. As the tech sector’s greenhouse gas emissions explode against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence boom and the clean energy incentives dry up under the Trump administration, Big Tech and Wall Street alike are funding a boom in natural gas, all under the guise of funding the future of clean energy. “ On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers ,” blared a Grist headline published earlier this week. The article details how private equity funds are making a killing on “energy transition” funds as electrification takes hold on a global scale and solar and wind power continue to see runaway growth trends, both current and projected. But many of these prominent energy transition funds prominently feature a fossil fuel and major contributors to greenhouse gas emissions on a global scale: natural gas. “‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” says Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the energy think tank Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition,” he went on to say. And those investors are not alone. Natural gas has been heavily promoted by the fossil fuel sector as a ‘bridge fuel’, serving as a stepping stone in the transition away from oil and coal toward 100 percent renewables. However, environmental experts question the wisdom of this approach and scientists have pushed back on the idea that natural gas is any cleaner than other fossil fuels, and calls for the abandonment of the ‘bridge fuel’ narrative have gained momentum in recent years. Methane, the principal ingredient in natural gas, is an extremely potent greenhouse gas. While methane breaks up much more quickly in the atmosphere than the better-known carbon dioxide, it is 80 times more potent at warming over a 20-year period. And peer–reviewed studies (like this one , this one , and this one ) are increasingly indicating that natural gas produces much, much more methane over its life cycle than previously thought. Plus, some studies even indicate that natural gas could be worse for the climate than coal when you include the emissions associated with the energy-intensive cooling, storage, and shipping processes associated with liquefied natural gas. However, the ‘bridge fuel’ argument still seems to hold major currency on Wall Street and in Silicon Valley. “I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, told Grist. For example, New York-based Blackstone, one of the world’s largest private equity firms, “is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel and the primary component of natural gas, is essential to the energy transition,” reports Grist. Meanwhile, Big Tech firms are causing a major natural gas boom around the country at the same time that they tout their backing of next-gen clean energy research, development, and adoption. Some of the biggest names in tech are building historically huge natural gas plants as we speak. Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States according to current specs, which include seven gas plants. title: Copper faces further slide after US vote: TD
summary: Copper could fall further as Democratic Party gains in the United States midterm elections weaken expectations for import tariffs.
body: Copper could fall further as Democratic Party gains in the United States midterm elections weaken expectations for import tariffs and raise doubts about projected demand from data centres, TD Securities says. Three-month copper futures on the London Metal Exchange declined to about $13,779 per tonne, or $6.25 per lb., by late afternoon Friday in London, their lowest level since July, data show. The metal has retreated from September’s intraday peak of almost $6.80 per lb. as traders reassess demand and the incentive to accumulate U.S. stockpiles. “We continue to expect the red metal to face further downside from here,” TD Securities managing director and global head of commodity strategy Bart Melek said in a note published Thursday. The risk is that copper loses some of the support from U.S. stockpiling before expected growth in data-centre consumption materializes. Mine disruptions and tight supplies outside the U.S. could nevertheless limit the decline, Fitch Group’s BMI research and data unit says. Democratic gains could increase resistance to power-hungry data centres, a source of expected copper demand growth, TD says. Affordability concerns ahead of the 2028 presidential vote could also reduce the appetite for aggressive copper tariffs, it says. “With many states slated for significant AI data center development turning blue, and opposition to new construction potentially growing, AI-driven copper demand could fall meaningfully short of current projections,” Melek wrote. “At the same time, many traders believe aggressive copper tariffs are now less likely with the Democratic Party controlling the U.S. Congress, and affordability the Achilles’ heel for the governing party heading into 2028.” U.S. copper inventories total about 1.6 million tonnes, TD estimates. Reduced stockpiling incentives and the disappearance of profitable price differences between American and overseas markets could halt additional inflows for a significant period. Slower imports would not necessarily mean an equivalent decline in industrial consumption. “As such, another $500 per tonne drift lower would not be a major surprise,” Melek wrote. Based on Thursday’s closing copper price of $13,843 per tonne in London, that would represent a drop of about 3.6%. BMI also sees tariff policy as the immediate catalyst, although it expects mine constraints and electrification demand to cushion any correction. It expects copper to average $13,500 per tonne this year and $12,900 in 2027. “U.S. tariff uncertainty remains the clearest near-term catalyst for copper, in our view,” BMI said in a report published Thursday. Washington’s July 2025 copper proclamation outlined possible refined copper duties of 15% from January 2027, rising to 30% in 2028, subject to a subsequent presidential determination. While Democratic gains could increase political pressure over the decision, the proclamation leaves it with the president — and the proposed levies remain unenacted. Separate 50% duties on certain semi-finished copper products and copper-intensive derivative products took effect in August 2025. Anticipation has nevertheless redirected trade. Higher Comex prices relative to London encouraged shipments into American warehouses before potential tariffs, reducing metal available elsewhere. Comex inventories rose about 62% from January through Wednesday, BMI reported, with those warehouses holding about 70% of global exchange copper stocks on Oct. 30. The dislocation overlays a concentrated supply chain. Chile supplied 68% of U.S. refined copper imports during 2021–24, followed by Canada at 16%, U.S. Geological Survey data show. China produced an estimated 14 million tonnes of refined copper in 2025, nearly half the global total. Chinese buyers are paying more to secure immediately available metal. body: Gold pulled back on Friday to test a trend support zone, establishing a lower daily high of $4,107 and a low of $4,027. This followed bullish signals from Thursday, including a reclaim of the 20-day moving average and downtrend line, plus a breakout above the recent lower swing high of $4,082 on the daily chart, which also represented a bullish reversal signal on the weekly chart. A higher weekly low was also generated this week at $3,875, supporting the potential for the beginning of a reversal in the current decline. The bullish signal was confirmed with a close above each of the resistance levels. Fridayâs pullback now provides an opportunity to assess whether those former resistance levels will hold as support. Since the recent decline took the form of a parallel trend channel, a breakout from that pattern also triggered on Thursday. The breakout hit resistance at $4,147 and closed in the lower half of the dayâs range, indicating that sellers were beginning to take control and raising the potential for a pullback to test prior resistance as support. That dynamic continued Friday. Bullish momentum that led to the breakout began from the recent low of $3,870, with a 7.15% advance completed at Thursdayâs high. That exceeded the previous three upswings that occurred since the August swing high at $4,697, the largest of which was an advance of 5.33%. This adds to the bullish technical evidence that buyers may be reclaiming control. It also suggests that by the time the prior swing high was recovered, gold was extended and prone to at least a small correction. This bullish price behavior indicates that the $3,870 low may have completed the corrective decline from the August high. If gold falls below Fridayâs low of $4,027, it could decline further to test support near the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement at $3,975, which is reinforced by a previous swing low. However, since the upside breakout signal from Thursday was confirmed with a close above the range, a recovery and continuation of the bullish reversal process is anticipated. Kitco provides the live gold price in U.S. dollars from the global spot market, updated every few seconds during trading hours. The table below breaks today's gold spot price in U.S. dollars into the units used in bullion and jewelry trade, converted live from the per-troy-ounce quote. Prices in U.S. dollars, based on the bid price of the global spot market. Tael refers to the Hong Kong tael (37.799 g). The spot price is the market price for one troy ounce of gold for immediate delivery, quoted in U.S. dollars. It is derived from the most actively traded gold futures contract together with over-the-counter dealing, and it moves nearly around the clock as trading follows the sun from New York to London, Zurich, Shanghai and Hong Kong. A troy ounce is 31.1034768 grams — about 10% heavier than the avoirdupois ounce used for groceries. Physical bullion products trade at a premium above spot that covers fabrication and distribution; the premium is proportionally larger on small items than on large bars. The chart above tracks this spot price. The currency selector converts the same underlying quote into other currencies using live exchange rates. The spot price is for gold delivered now; a futures price is for gold delivered on a set date in the future, traded on exchanges such as COMEX. The two normally differ by the cost of carrying gold to that date — storage, insurance and interest — which is why futures usually trade slightly above spot, a condition called contango . When futures trade below spot — backwardation — it signals unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery, and it’s rare enough in gold that it makes news when it happens. The price on this page is the spot price; quotes you see for "gold futures" refer to the most active COMEX contract. Real interest rates and the Federal Reserve. Gold pays no yield, so its strongest headwind is a high real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate — and its strongest tailwind is a falling one. Fed rate decisions, inflation reports and Treasury yields are the events most likely to move the gold price on any given day. Inflation and currency debasement. Gold's reputation as an inflation hedge is best understood over long horizons: across decades, gold has broadly preserved purchasing power as paper currencies lost it, which is why demand rises when investors expect sustained inflation or growing government debt. Over shorter periods the relationship is looser — in an inflation spike, what matters most is how the Fed responds, which is why real interest rates (above) are the better day-to-day guide. The U.S. dollar. Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to lift the gold price and a stronger dollar tends to weigh on it — even when nothing about gold itself has changed. To see how much of a move is gold versus the dollar, the Kitco Global Index (KGX) tracks gold’s value measured against a basket of major currencies with the U.S. dollar’s influence stripped out. body: Brent crude oil is heading for its biggest weekly percentage decline since the COVID-19 pandemic, with prices falling approximately 16% as investors increasingly anticipate a de-escalation of the US-Israeli war against Iran. January Brent futures traded near $98.60 per barrel at 11:29 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hovered around $91. Brent's projected weekly decline would also be its largest in dollar terms in LSEG records dating to 1988. However, the weekly figures remain provisional until trading closes. The selloff accelerated after the November 3 US midterm elections, when Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Investors interpreted the result as increasing political pressure for a negotiated settlement with Iran, potentially allowing additional Gulf oil exports to return to international markets. Brent plunged more than 8% on Wednesday alone, reaching a two-month low near $94.62. The move followed an earlier decline below $103 , when President Donald Trump indicated that Washington had no immediate plans for additional strikes. Oil's reversal is particularly dramatic because Brent traded above $116 in late October following tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz . That earlier rally reflected fears of prolonged export disruptions rather than an immediate shortage of equivalent size. As Coinpaper explained in its analysis of oil prices and OPEC supply , futures markets respond to expected supply conditions, not simply barrels currently available. Despite falling prices, the Middle East's physical supply risks have not disappeared. Britain's maritime security agency UKMTO reported that attacks on oil-carrying vessels remained close to record levels. A seafarer was killed following an explosion aboard an oil-products tanker, while further incidents renewed concerns about shipping safety. The disruptions follow earlier US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island , which temporarily pushed crude prices higher. Meanwhile, OPEC+ agreed to maintain September's required production levels for December rather than announce another increase. The decision reinforces the distinction between official output targets and oil actually reaching buyers. Earlier Iran peace negotiations and the OPEC+ production freeze demonstrated how quickly diplomatic expectations can outweigh production decisions. Brent's immediate resistance sits around $100, followed by $103–$105 if prices sustain a recovery. However, a stronger rebound toward $110 would likely require renewed supply concerns or a significant deterioration in negotiations. title: Sell-Side Analysts Fail To Adequately Adjust Stock Forecasts After Fed Meetings - Eurasia Review
body: When the U.S. Federal Reserve announces a change in its interest rate, consumers expect shifts in borrowing costs elsewhere and potential price adjustments for things like housing and some consumer goods. New research however shows that stock market analysts generally give a collective “meh” around the time of Fed meetings when it comes to forecasting how much stocks will trade for in the future, called a price target. Despite dozens of Fed meetings between 2000 and 2020 where interest rates were either raised or lowered, researchers at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management found that price targets among analysts working at investment houses and brokerages were only adjusted for 18.5 percent of companies in the two weeks before and after Fed meetings. As a result, those targets — which investors use when deciding to buy or sell stocks — lose accuracy after a Fed meeting, either overpredicting future stock prices when rates rise or underpredicting them when rates drop. In practice, stock prices on average fall in response to interest rate hikes and rise when rates relax. Comparing actual stock prices to what was forecast, the researchers found that prediction inaccuracy increased by about 13 percent when the Fed hiked rates and by more than 16 percent when rates dropped. That analysts are making such mistakes is “not surprising,” said lead author Junhao Liu, a senior accounting lecturer, which is equivalent to an assistant professor, at the University of Melbourne who conducted the research while completing his PhD in the Rotman School’s accounting doctoral program. “Analysts always make mistakes, whether intentional or unintentional.” The driver of this particular error, show Dr. Liu and his co-researchers, is a failure to adjust the discount rate analysts use as part of their forecasting. Expressed as a percentage, the discount rate accounts for things like risk, interest rates and the cost of tying up money over the longer term and translates a stock’s future value into today’s money. Not surprisingly, forecast inaccuracy was heightened for companies with high exposure to interest rates, such as financial and highly leveraged companies. It was less pronounced for investment houses with macro-economists on staff who presumably could provide more precise guidance on potential impacts of interest rate changes. Even having highly rated crackerjack analysts did not help after a Fed rate increase, which happened 29 times during the studied period. Those hot performers did however show less inaccuracy around rate decreases, which happened 28 times. The findings highlight “potential limitations in how some of the most important capital market intermediaries interpret and act upon fundamental macroeconomic information,” said Ole-Kristian Hope, who is the Deloitte Professor of Accounting at the Rotman School who supervised Dr. Liu’s research. The study was also co-authored by Rotman accounting PhD graduate Mingyue Zhang, now an assistant professor in financial reporting at the University of Waterloo. While the research did not delve into why analysts fall short in adjusting their target prices, Dr. Liu speculated that it may be because they are just being conservative — not wanting to make changes because these will have consequences elsewhere — may be unable to process the exact effect of the interest rate change, or they may feel incentivized to maintain high price forecasts in the face of an interest rate hike. Given the wild rise in interest rates following the COVID-19 pandemic, the findings could be helpful to investors trying to make sense of the market and to analysts striving for better accuracy in an era of dramatic monetary policy shifts, the research concludes. The study appeared in the September 2026 issue of the Journal of Banking & Finance. Eurasia Review is an independent international news and analysis platform founded in 2009. World Bank's Banga: Availability of capital 'not really an issue' as AI demand drives up borrowing costs
summary: World Bank President Ajay Banga came on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 27, 2026.
body: World Bank President Ajay Banga said on Tuesday that capital remained available despite concerns of artificial intelligence sending interest rates higher. "It's not really an issue," Banga said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box." Banga said the World Bank mobilized $112 billion last year, around three times the amount recorded three years prior. He said investors may be concerned about circular financing and the business model tied to AI. But Banga told CNBC that emerging markets are not running into the same hesitancy because the investments focus more on infrastructure like bridges and roads. These countries also look at smaller-scale uses of AI, according to Banga. Banga said developed counterparts look to funding to support large use cases, which he described as the "exact opposite" need. The World Bank leader also said that the private capital it oversees does not go to governments. As a result, the organization can avoid fears of looming debt crises and challenges related to rising bond yields within some countries. "In general, I still believe that AI is going to be transformative and profitable," Banga said. "But everybody sees bumps in the road from here to there, and no one knows when the next bump will come." Banga's comments come ahead of a string of interest rate decisions from central banks around the world. Economists and monetary policymakers across the globe have been attempting to gauge how the widespread adoption of AI impacts demand for capital and employment. The financial institution, which was founded in 1944, aims to end poverty and support economic prosperity through global partnerships and funding. Before taking the top job at the bank, Banga was vice chair at General Atlantic and CEO of Mastercard .

title: Fed rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey
summary: The CNBC Fed Survey shows that 93% of respondent expect a pause at the Federal Reserve meeting taking place this week.
body: The Federal Reserve has considerable work to do. But it's not going to do it in October. That's the key finding in CNBC's latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, which showed that 93% expect a pause at the Fed meeting taking place this week and 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. And more than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes. "Their hesitancy to raise rates is unfathomable after an extended period of monetary and fiscal generosity, with nominal GDP running 6-8%, and when the leading indicators of inflation are uniformly warm to hot,'' said Richard Bernstein, global head of macro investing at Janus Henderson Investors. A plurality of 40% say the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem . That compares with 27% who say the Fed does not need to slow the economy and 23% who say the Fed has to slow the economy only somewhat. The survey, which CNBC conducts before every Fed meeting, found that 70% see the inflation problem as broader than just the rising price of energy. The U.S. crude oil benchmark is forecast to be at $88 a barrel six months from now, up from $82 in the September survey, but below the current level of $101. Asked what the Fed should do at the current meeting, 30% said it should hike rates now. At least two Fed voters are expected by survey respondents to dissent from the decision to keep rates unchanged. "The aggregate demand data (probably north of 7%...) and the inflation data point to the strong need to hike rates,'' wrote John Ryding, chief economic advisor for Brean Capital, LLC. "The Iran War is intensifying, real wages are falling, interest rates are rising, and the AI-fueled stock market looks shaky," wrote Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Inflation is high, but there's little sign it is becoming entrenched. This isn't the time for more Fed rate hikes. Amid numerous shocks and challenges — including high inflation , expected Fed rate hikes and a continuation of high oil prices — respondents still see economic growth remaining above potential, or the level of growth that doesn't lead to inflation or deflation. Forecasts of GDP for this year rose to 2.4%. They ticked down slightly since the last survey but still hover above potential at 2.2% for 2027. Growth in 2025 came in at 2.05%. Respondents in aggregate put the risk of the U.S. entering a recession in the next year at 26%, down from 29% in the last survey. The outlook for the S&P 500 stayed stable for this year at around 7,600 but moved down to 8,033 for next year from 8,274 in the prior survey. The index closed at 7,676 Monday. Unemployment is forecast to remain steady at 4.2% through the remainder of the year but rise to 4.4% in 2027. The Consumer Price Index is seen ticking down to 3.6% from the current pace of 3.7% in September but fall meaningfully next year to 2.6%. The biggest risks: a continuation of the Iran war and the bursting of the artificial-intelligence bubble . "Fed Chair Warsh, in all of his future conversations with President Trump, need to repeat this mantra: the quickest way to bring down inflation in the U.S. is to end tariffs and end the war in Iran," said Rob Morgan, senior vice president and market strategist at MOSAIC. When it comes to high bond yields , respondents in almost equal percentages say the culprits are high inflation, high growth, large amounts of debt issuance and expectations for a higher Fed funds rate. Asked specifically about which supply was the bigger source of the problem, 50% said government debt and 13% said debt to fund the AI buildout. But a third said both had contributed equally to the rise in yields. On average, respondents see the 10-year yield remaining above 5% this year and dropping slightly to 4.8% in 2027 "With stubborn inflation amid energy and trade pressures… benchmark U.S. Treasury bond yields above 5% represent a new band, not an anomaly," wrote Subodh Ku

title: Gold Posts Biggest Weekly Gain Since August as Wall Street Analysts Split on Outlook - BigGo Finance
body: Global gold prices ended the trading week up about 5%, marking the strongest weekly advance since August, after US midterm election results pushed the dollar and US Treasury yields lower. Still, the latest survey showed Wall Street analysts have yet to reach a consensus on the direction of the precious metal next week, while retail investors appeared decidedly more optimistic. Spot gold opened the week at $3,875.21/oz on Sunday evening US time. The rally extended as cooling oil prices eased inflation concerns, along with bargain-hunting after a steep decline the prior week. The recovery stalled on Tuesday when stronger-than-expected US economic data lifted both Treasury yields and the greenback, at one point dragging gold below $3,900/oz. The turning point came on Tuesday evening and Wednesday, when the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress. The outcome fueled expectations of legislative gridlock and the possibility of reduced government borrowing, easing concerns about the fiscal deficit. Treasury yields and the dollar fell sharply, providing support for gold to reclaim the $4,000/oz level and climb to a weekly peak of $4,147.02/oz on Thursday. The rally was capped when US equities, particularly technology stocks, sold off sharply, forcing investors to liquidate assets to cover losses. The trigger was reportedly concern that Democratic control of Congress would bring tighter oversight of artificial intelligence companies, amid growing opposition to data center expansion. On Friday, selling pressure intensified after the US October nonfarm payrolls report showed 165,000 new jobs, well above forecasts, and an unemployment rate that fell to 4.1%. The upbeat data reinforced expectations that the Fed could continue raising rates in December, supporting the dollar and pushing short-term yields higher. At one point gold retreated to near $4,030/oz before paring some losses and closing the week just below $4,070.1/oz. The outlook for next week is notably divided. Of 13 experts surveyed by a precious metals website, only four, or 31%, said gold would rise. Five, or 38%, forecast a decline, while the remaining four expected the market to move sideways or were unclear on direction. The near-even split reflects cautious sentiment after a week of sharp swings. On the opposite side, an online poll with 212 votes recorded 143 respondents, or 68%, expecting gold to continue higher; 32 forecast a decline and 37 expected the precious metal to consolidate sideways. Retail investor confidence was clearly bolstered after the midweek rebound, in contrast to analysts' hesitation. Data from ANZ showed central bank demand for gold remains solid. In the third quarter, these institutions were net buyers of 321 tonnes, the fastest pace since late 2024, driven by geopolitical concerns and fiscal discipline. However, the same report also noted that lower government borrowing could weaken one source of gold demand. On the outlook, Nam Yong-soo, head of the ETF division at Korea Investment Management, said that through year-end, ahead of the Fed's rate decision, international gold prices will fluctuate with a floor around $4,000/oz. According to him, the moment the Fed ends its rate-hiking cycle and real rates cool will mark a turning point for the next leg higher, while noting factors to watch including US real rates, the monetary policy path, oil prices and the won/USD exchange rate. Kim Min-soo, head of global ETF management at Mirae Asset, said short-term volatility may increase after the midterm elections but gold still has considerable upside. He pointed out that rate-hike concerns have largely been priced in, while central bank and global gold ETF buying remains intact, and historically the precious metal has tended to rise before a tightening cycle actually ends. title: Silver may rally 40% by Dhanteras 2027, but experts advise caution amid near-term weakness - Moneycontrol.com

Dhanteras is traditionally seen as an occasion to welcome wealth and abundance, with many investors using the auspicious day to add gold and silver to their portfolios. Commodity experts now estimate that silver could rise to Rs 2,65,000 in one year, or at least 40 percent by Dhanteras 2027, and gold by 20-30 percent during the same period. According to Renisha Chainani, Chief Research Officer at Augmont, silver, currently at Rs 1.88 lakh per kg (around $52/oz), could gain 40 percent to reach approximately Rs 2.65 lakh (around $75). Gold, currently at Rs 1.45 lakh per 10 grams (around $4,100/oz), could rise 20 percent to nearly Rs 1.75 lakh by Diwali 2027, equivalent to around $4,950/oz internationally. "These targets imply the ratio easing to about 67. In India, the rupee near 94.5 and the 15 percent import duty should keep domestic prices firm," Chainani said. Silver has fallen to a near one-year low since November 2025 as elevated oil prices, strong US economic data and persistent inflation concerns fuel expectations of higher interest rates for longer, lifting real yields and weakening demand for non-yielding precious metals, such as silver. The metal slipped 0.52 percent to $52.10 per ounce today (Nov. 6) on Comex, while domestic silver spot price posted a marginal loss to Rs 1,82,453 per kilogram on the Multi Commodity Exchange. Nirpendra Yadav, Sr. Research Analyst at Bonanza Portfolio, estimates that silver will likely remain volatile in the next 12 months, with a cautious near-term bias but scope for a gradual recovery if monetary and investment conditions become more supportive. "Silver is still struggling to establish a durable uptrend. Technically, for the 6-12 months horizon, silver could see a recovery if gold resumes its upward trend and investment flows return to precious metals," Yadav said. He estimates that if silver prices break and sustain above $62, then prices may move towards $70, which would act as crucial resistance, and further upside is possible only above this level. Meanwhile, a decisive break below $47 may keep silver prices under pressure. On MCX, Rs 1,60,000 will act as a crucial support level, while Rs 215,000 will act as a hurdle. "However, the short- to mid-term trend has become down, so silver prices may remain sideways to downside or may trade in a range for the upcoming months," Yadav said. Commodity analysts reason that the biggest near-term risk is the interest-rate and bond-yield environment. Higher US real yields and a stronger dollar tend to reduce the appeal of non-yielding precious metals. Silver is particularly vulnerable because it has a higher beta to gold and tends to magnify both upward and downward moves. If expectations of further monetary tightening persist, silver could continue to underperform gold in the near term. Conversely, any shift towards lower interest rates, softer bond yields or a weaker US dollar could trigger a meaningful recovery. Investors should closely monitor US real yields and Federal Reserve policy, the US dollar, gold prices, and the gold-silver ratio, as these will remain key drivers of silver investment demand. At the same time, developments in Chinese and Indian physical demand, solar-panel silver consumption, ETF or ETP flows, exchange inventories, recycling and mine supply will provide clues about the underlying physical market. Sustained investment flows could tighten the market again, while rising inventories and continued ETF outflows would signal that the earlier supply squeeze is unwinding. According to Swapnil Aggarwal, Director of VSRK Capital, the silver outlook remains Cautious for 2026-end, with recovery likely only in the long term. body: Cloudflare ( NET ) sank 8% today, ahead of its third-quarter report, as the AI selloff that hammered chip stocks spread to software. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress after a campaign in which candidates from both parties took aim at AI data centers. As Yahoo Finance’s Jared Blikre put it , “The stocks that had the best year are now the ones with the most to lose.” Cloudflare had climbed sharply in 2026 , and it’s on pace for its worst day since May. Cloudflare’s tie to AI data centers is mostly indirect. CEO Matthew Prince’s rule is to “invest behind demand,” adding servers to its network after customers show up. And its CFO said last year that no AI-native customer made up more than 2% of revenue. Okta ( OKTA ) , down 11% with no news of its own, shows the whole group is getting sold.
